# Book Pages 174–209 # Constituted Text Only; Critical Apparatus Removed ## Section 2. Genealogy (Vaṃśa) | Chapter 2 | A. (Bd. II. 3.1–131; Vā. 66.1–152.)
The sages said:
"Tell us in detail the origin of the gods, the dānavas, and the daityas in every respect during the Vaivasvata interval!"
Sūta said:
I shall now proclaim the very origin of Dharma; listen to it:
Arundhatī, Vasu, Yāmī, Lambā, Bhānu, and Marutvatī.
Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and likewise Viśvā; || 2 ||
Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave these ten as lawful wives to Dharma;
the Sādhyas were the sons of Dharma, and twelve Sādhyas were born. || 3 ||
The highly fortunate ones named Sādhyas, born of Chanda, are partakers of the sacrifice;
those who know the gods designate them as gods superior to [the other] gods. || 4 ||
Indeed, the Jaya deities were created by Brahmā from his mouth with the desire for progeny;
they are all remembered here as being composed of mantras throughout the Manvantaras. 5.
The New Moon sacrifice and the Full Moon sacrifice, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara [Sāmans], as well as perception, discernment, intention, and purpose. (6)
The knower, the known, and likewise the mind and the sacrifice—these indeed are the celebrated names of those Victors (Jinas). || 7 ||
By the curse of Brahmā, they were born again as the unconquered ones (Ajitas) in the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara];
in the Svārociṣa [Manvantara] they were the Tuṣitas, and in the Uttama [Manvantara] they were the Satyas. || 8 ||
In the Tāmasa Manvantara, they were named Haris; in the Revata interval, Vaikuṇṭhas; and in the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, the gods known as Sādhyas were born from Chanda. || 9 ||
The highly fortunate sons of Dharma, who were the twelve gods to be propitiated, were formerly known as the Anusūyas during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu. || 10 ||
In the Svārociṣa interval, those gods of great power who had passed away spoke among themselves concerning the Cākṣuṣa interval: "They are indeed named Tuṣitas. || 11 ||
When only a small portion remained of him, the Tuṣita gods then said:
"Let us enter this very highly fortunate Sādhyā. || 12 ||
"We shall exist in the Manvantara; that will be for our welfare. Having spoken thus, they all [remained] during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu. || 13 ||
From that Svāyambhuva Dharma, twelve [sons] were born again;
indeed, Nara and Nārāyaṇa were born there once more. || 14 ||
Vipaścit was the Indra, and Satya as well as Hari;
these two were formerly the Tuṣita gods during the Svārociṣa interval. || 15 ||
But when they are to be accomplished as the Tuṣitas, these names are proclaimed:
Mano, Anumantṛ, Prāṇa, Nara, and the vigorous Apāna. (16)
Citti, Haya, Naya, Haṃsa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa;
Prabhava and Vibhu—thus the twelve Sādhyas were born. || 17 ||
In the previous Svāyambhuva Manvantara, and then again in the Svārociṣa Manvantara, there were those same names for the Tuṣitas; learn them now once more.
Prāṇa, apāna, udāna, samāna, and vyāna;
as well as sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch, intellect, and mind. || 19 ||
These names were indeed formerly remembered as those of the Tuṣitas;
the Vasus are known as the sons of Vasa, and they are recorded as the younger brothers of the Sādhyas.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anala, Anila, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. || 21 ||
Dhara’s son was Draviṇa, as well as Hutahavyavaha;
and Dhruva’s son, O dear one, was Kāla, the destroyer of the worlds. || 22 ||
The lord Varcas and Budha, the enlighteners among the planets, were both born under Rohiṇī; they are renowned throughout the three worlds. || 23 ||
And the three sons of Candramas were Dhārā, Ūrmi, and Kalila;
likewise, the sons of Āpa were Vaitaṇḍya, Śama, and Śānta.
Skanda and Sanatkumāra were born from a portion of his splendor;
however, Kumāra, the son of Agni, was born from a clump of reeds.
Śākha, Viśākha, and Naigameya were born after him.
Anila’s wife was Śivā, and her son was Manojava.
And the two sons of Anila were Avijñātagati and [Vijñātagati]. They know the son of Pratyūṣa to be the ṛṣi named Devala. || 27 ||
Devala also had two sons who were patient and wise;
and Bṛhaspati’s sister was an excellent woman who remained a celibate.
Having attained perfection through yoga, she wanders throughout the entire world unattached;
she was indeed the wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus. || 29 ||
From her was born Viśvakarman, the son and lord of artisans;
he is the creator of all crafts and the carpenter of the gods.
He is the maker and the cause of all ornaments;
he also creates the celestial chariots of all the deities. || 31 ||
And human artisans subsist upon the crafts of him [Viśvakarman].
Furthermore, ten renowned Viśvedevas were born from Viśvā: || 32 ||
Kratu, Dakṣa, Śravas, Satya, Kāla, Kāma, Muni,
Kuruvān, Prabhava, and Rocamāna— these are the ten.
These auspicious sons of Dharma were born of Surā as Viśvā;
the Marutvats were born of Marutvatī, and the Bhānus are recorded as the offspring of Bhānu. || 34 ||
And from Muhūrtā, Ghoṣa was born;
and from Saṃkalpā, the wise Saṃkalpa himself was born. || 35 ||
All the serpent-lineages that depend upon those three paths were born from Arundhatī throughout the entire realm of the earth. || 36 ||
This eternal creation of Dharma has been fully described;
as well as the muhūrtas and the lunar days (tithis), together with their presiding deities, O you of virtuous vows.
I shall proclaim their names; listen to me as I speak!
The division of day and night is based upon the constellations. || 38 ||
The muhūrtas, all the lunar mansions, and likewise the divisions of day and night, as well as the sixty-four parts of a day and night, are thus recorded. || 39 ||
Due to the specific movement of the sun throughout all the seasons at all times, those who know the Vedas therefore desire this path on the festival days (parvan). || 40 ||
In times when no specific distinction is made, they should be known by the measurement of the sun:
Raudra, Sārpa, Maitra, Pitrya, and Vāsava. (41)
Then the Āpya and the Vaiśvadeva; the Brāhma is situated at midday;
likewise the Prājāpatya, the Aindra, and those of Indra-Agni and Nirṛti. || 42 ||
Vāruṇa, Aryaman, and Bhaga are likewise dependent upon the day;
these are the muhūrtas of the day created by the Maker of Light.
They are to be known by their measure according to the specific shadow of the gnomon (śaṅku):
those presided over by Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the Aśvins, and Yama. (44)
The Āgneya should also be known, as well as the Prājāpatya;
likewise the Brāhma, Saumya, Āditya, Bārhaspatya, and Vaiṣṇava. || 45 ||
The Sāvitra, the Tvāṣṭra, and the Vāyavya—this is the summary;
these are the fifteen Muhūrtas of the night, as stated in their proper order. || 46 ||
The movements and risings of the moon are to be known as the quarter-hour (pādika) nāḍīs;
these are the temporal states, and these muhūrtas are remembered as deities. || 47 ||
For all the grahas, exactly three locations have been ordained:
the southern, the northern, and the middle; one should know them in their respective order. || 48 ||
The Sthāna-Jāradgava is in the middle; likewise, Airāvata is in the north, and Vaiśvānara is specified here as being in the south according to the truth. || 49 ||
The path known as Nāgavīthī consists of Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, and the region of Yama;
likewise, that called Gajavīthī comprises Brāhma, Saumya, and Ārdrā. || 50 ||
Likewise, when Puṣya and Āśleṣā are with the Sun, the path is considered Airāvatī;
these three paths indeed are called the Northern Course. || 51 ||
Pūrvaphalgunī and Uttaraphalgunī, as well as Maghā, are known as the path of the Bull (ārṣabhī);
likewise, Hasta, Citrā, and Svātī are designated as the path of the Cow (govīthī). || 52 ||
Jyeṣṭhā, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā are known as the Jāradgavī path;
these three paths are called the middle course. || 53 ||
The root [constellation] consists of Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā, which is designated as the Ajavīthī; likewise, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Mārgī (Pūrvabhādrapadā), and Śatabhiṣak. || 54 ||
Vaiśvānarī and Revatī are proclaimed [to be the constellations] in Bhādrapada;
these three are remembered as the paths (vīthīs), and those three paths are called the southern path (dakṣiṇamārga). This is indeed the southern path according to the wise.
Dakṣa gave twenty-seven maidens to Soma;
all of them, known by the names of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), are celebrated in the science of astronomy (jyotiṣa). || 56 ||
Their offspring were radiant and possessed immeasurable splendor;
as for those daughters who remained, Kaśyapa then took them as his wives.
There are fourteen highly fortunate ones, all of whom are mothers of the world:
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Ariṣṭhā, and likewise Surasā; || 58 ||
Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, Irā, Kadrū, and Muni—who was likewise a knower of dharma—were their daughters; learn now of their progeny! || 59 ||
In the past Cāriṣṇava interval, those twelve best of gods who were known as the Vaikuṇṭhas became the Sādhyas during the Cākṣuṣa interval. || 60 ||
For when this interval had arrived once more under Vaivasvata, those who had propitiated Aditi gathered together and spoke to one another: || 61 ||
Having indeed entered this most illustrious Aditi,
during this very Vaivasvata interval, you shall [arise] through yoga with half of my splendor.
"Let us become her sons; that will be for our welfare.
[For those born of Aditi, there shall be the status of Ādityas.
Having spoken thus, they all [remained] during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu. || 63 ||
The twelve Ādityas were born again from Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci;
indeed, Śatakratu and Viṣṇu were likewise born once more.
For in this Vaivasvata interval, there were the two gods Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
indeed, even for those gods, birth and death are said to occur. || 65 ||
Just as in this world there are both the rising and the setting of the sun, so it is with Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, and the high-souled Bhava. || 66 ||

Because they were attached to that which is perceived through sight and heard through tradition—characterized by sound and the rest—and to the eightfold [powers] beginning with *aṇiman*, therefore those gods were born. || 67 ||
Thus, this passion for sense objects is recorded as the cause of rebirth.
Born through the curse of Brahmā during the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara], the Jayas remained unconquered. || 68 ||
In the Svārociṣa [Manvantara], they were the Tuṣitas; in the Uttama, the Satyas;
in the Tāmasa, the gods were born as the Haris; and in the Cākṣuṣa, indeed. (69)
The Vaikuṇṭhas were in the Cākṣuṣa [Manvantara], and the Sādhyas and Ādityas are [the gods] in the present one.
Furthermore, Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga; || 70 ||
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is recorded as the tenth;
after him Tvaṣṭṛ, and then Viṣṇu, who is not the least, though born last. || 71 ||
Thus, these twelve Ādityas are remembered as the sons of Kaśyapa.
Surabhī gave birth to the eleven Rudras from Kaśyapa. (72)
Through the grace of Mahādeva and purified by ascetic penance, she [worshipped] Aṅgāraka, as well as Sarpa, Nirṛti, and Sadasaspati. || 73 ||
Ajaikapād and Ahirbudhnya—these two, as well as Jvara, Bhuvana, Īśvara, Mṛtyu, and the renowned Kapālī. (74)
Surabhi gave birth to these eleven gods, the Rudras who are the lords of the three worlds, through her great and fierce ascetic penance.
Then he begot two other daughters, both of them fragrant:
the fortunate Rohiṇī and the illustrious Gāndharvī. || 76 ||
Under Rohiṇī were born four daughters renowned throughout the world:
Surūpā, Haṃsakālī, Bhadrā, and likewise Kāmadughā. || 77 ||
Hamsakālī gave birth to cows that yielded every desire, Surūpā to two sons, and Mahiṣā to buffaloes; from Bhadrā, however, were born the Avijātis. || 78 ||
The highly fortunate sons of Gāndharvī, however, were the famous horses, beginning with Uccaiḥśravas; they were born as sky-goers, swift as thought. || 79 ||
White, red, tawny, dappled, green, and silver—these horses, said to be the mounts of the gods, have their origin in the Gandharvas. || 80 ||
Furthermore, from Surabhi was born the glorious bull Candraprabha, wearing garlands, possessing a hump, radiant, and originating from the abode of nectar. || 81 ||
"With Surabhi's consent, that banner was given to him as Māheśvara.
Thus, these sons of Kaśyapa are celebrated as the Rudras and Ādityas. || 82 ||
The Dharmaputras, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and likewise the Vasus are remembered as such.
Furthermore, there were sixteen offspring here from the wives of Ariṣṭanemi.
For the learned Bahuputra, four types of lightning are recorded;
those born of Pratyāṅgirasa are the most excellent, consisting of Ṛks honored by the Brahman-sages. || 84 ||
The divine weapons are said to belong to the celestial sage Kṛśāśva;
indeed, these are born once again at the end of a thousand yugas. || 85 ||
All the hosts of gods and the thirty-three Brahmins born of the Vedas—for these gods as well, cessation and origination are taught. || 86 ||
Just as both the rising and the setting of the sun occur in this world, so do these hosts of gods come into being age after age. || 87 ||
The seers said:
"The Sādhyas, the Vasus, the Viśvedevas, and likewise the Rudras and Ādityas, are renowned for their noble birth, their powers, and their deeds. (88)
We wish to know the distinction between Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, and the high-souled Bhava, and which among them excels the other. || 89 ||
He from whom one originates, he in whom one is established, and among them, he who is indeed the eldest, the middlemost, and the youngest; || 90 ||

Tell us all of this—who among them was the principal one, and who was subordinate to them; who was great by reason of his deeds, his birth, and his power—for you indeed know each thing as it truly is! || 91 ||
Sūta said:
In this regard, I shall describe to you the distinction among them that is traditionally remembered; listen to me as I speak of the difference between Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra! || 92 ||
These bodies of the Self-existent One are declared to be of the nature of passion (rājasī), darkness (tāmasī), and goodness (sāttvikī); they manifest from time to time. || 93 ||

O best of the twice-born, it is impossible to state the difference between these [grammatical operations], because they are bound together by the rules of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, and because they are linked by a twofold favor. || 94 ||
O twice-born ones, I shall explain here, according to my ability, the manifestation and cessation of the qualities and the growth of the bodies; listen to that! || 95 ||
Among these, the Brāhmī is characterized by rajas; that which is called Kālā is known to be tāmasī;
and the Pauruṣī is indeed sāttvikī. Understand now their respective functions!
Of these, it is the rājasī alone that produces offspring in every way. || 96 ||
One [form] abiding in the ocean is the *sāttvika* one, which bestows grace;
the other is the *tāmasa* one, which in due time casts down and devours all creatures. || 97 ||
But when he is overwhelmed by passion (rajas) and is born as a Brāhmaṇa, then his sattvic designation as "Puruṣa" ceases. || 98 ||
When he becomes the self of Time through the excess of darkness (tamas), then his state called Brāhma ceases and the Rājasa state arises. || 99 ||
But when a person becomes a Lord due to the predominance of *sattva*, then that [state] of his is called "Time," and it indeed does not cease to exist again. || 100 ||
Gradually, for him who exists throughout the three worlds through the acts of creation, favor, and restraint, his form, name, and activity cease. || 101 ||
When one becomes Brahman, then an interval is said to exist;
yet when the person is Brahman, he is not truly that person.
Just as a gem reflects various colors within a crystal, so it is here. || 102 ||
Due to its stainlessness and by virtue of its basis, it would possess that color and be colored by that. || 103 ||
Then, by virtue of its qualities, there is a spontaneous attraction toward that Self-existent One;
this is declared to be the illustration of both unity and diversity.
Just as fire [is manifested] by virtue of fuel...
But he who is one becomes manifold; likewise, that Grandfather exists as one among his various forms.
Just as a single cloud, having become one,
remains divided in its form and color, so too [does he].
Likewise, by the power of the qualities (guṇas),
he becomes one, two, or even threefold through the dissolution of his forms. || 105 ||
The one who is Brahmā, the one who is the End-maker (Śiva), and the Puruṣa—these three are known as the three fierce bodies of the Self-existent One (Svayambhū). || 106 ||
They are known as Brāhmī, Pauruṣī, and Kālākhyā.
Among them, that which is Rājasī is his body; indeed, it is the producer of progeny. || 107 ||
That which is called Kālī is tāmasī and causes the destruction of progeny; that which is Pauruṣī is sāttvikī and is remembered as bestowing grace. || 108 ||
From a portion of Brahmā’s Rajas quality, Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, came into being;
and from that which was his Tamas quality, which brings about the end, Bhava arose as its portion. || 109 ||

That which is characterized by *sattva* and *puruṣa*, a portion of that is called Viṣṇu; those bodies of the Self-born One are remembered as the lords (*īśvaras*) throughout the three worlds. || 110 ||
For he who brings about various states of time for the sake of diverse purposes, having created all beings as Brahmā and having favored them as Viṣṇu; || 111 ||
Favored by Vaiṣṇavī, they are again consumed by Raudrī;
as the one Self-existent Time, he indeed effects the three through the three. || 112 ||
"He creates, favors, and likewise withdraws all beings"—thus have these three forms of the Self-born (Svayambhū) been described. || 113 ||
They are remembered as belonging to Prajāpati, to Rudra, and to Viṣṇu;
these bodies are recorded in the Veda, in the Dharmaśāstra, and in ancient tradition. 114.
By the wise sages who delight in Sāṃkhya and Yoga, who perceive the identity of the distinct [principles], who know the power of his manifestation, and who see the ultimate reality. || 115 ||
Regarding these [elements], these various beings, divided by oneness and by difference, speak with a dualistic vision, saying, "This is supreme, this is not. || 116 ||
Some say Brahmā is the cause; some say Prajāpati; some declare Śiva to be the supreme, and others likewise Viṣṇu. || 117 ||
Born of ignorance, attached through passion, and devoid of discernment, they fail to consider reality, time, place, the task at hand, and their own actions. (118)
For these deities are traditionally remembered as the causes for various matters here;
by praising one, however, one praises them all. || 119 ||
He who censures one among them censures all;
he who knows that One Person, him they call a teacher of Brahman. || 120 ||
Therefore, one who possesses discernment should not harbor malice toward the deities;
for it is impossible to fully know the Lord as he abides in his sovereign power. || 121 ||
He who, being of a single self, becomes threefold and deludes all creatures—
people wander within the interval between these three.
Those who desire to know, those who investigate, those who are attached, the wicked, and the senseless—seeing things with divided perspectives, they say, "This is supreme, this is not. || 123 ||
The Yātudhānas and the Piśācas are not distinct;
they are one, though appearing as separate.
And having become [that] himself, he remains. || 124 ||
Who is able to know whether they are one or many, since he, having created them, favors them and likewise devours them? (127)
Because its nature consists of the qualities (guṇas) throughout the three periods of time, it is therefore called one.
[It manifests as] Rudra, Brahmā, Indra, the world-protectors, the sages, and the Manus. || 128 ||
The twice-born call that one God, Nārāyaṇa, by many names;
his bodies are those of Prajāpati, Rudra, and indeed Viṣṇu. (129)
Indeed, throughout the Manvantaras, these three revolve again and again;
and other Kṣetrajñas also are born from the grace of this All-pervading Lord.
Learn now also of those who are born equal to them in splendor, fame, intelligence, sacred learning, and strength. (131)
From a portion of the Rajasic Brahma, Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, was born;
and from a portion of that same [Brahma] belonging to the Tamasic aspect, Rudra is said to be the essence of Time. || 132 ||
At that time, Viṣṇu became the sacrifice through his sattvic portion as the Puruṣa;
these three bodies of his, born of his portions, are the Brahmas throughout the three periods of time. || 133 ||
In this world, during the various Manvantaras, they return again and again to create;
throughout all the Manvantaras, so do all beings, both stationary and moving. || 133 ||
Produced once at the beginning of the aeon, they remain here until the end of the restraint; but whenever the end of the aeon arrives, Rudra withdraws all living beings. || 133 ||
Becoming Time (Kāla), that Rudra again withdraws all creatures when the end of the aeon has arrived; he is the seven-rayed sun.
Becoming the Saṃvartaka sun, he indeed burns the three worlds;
Viṣṇu is the one who bestows grace upon all creatures. Viṣṇu constantly shows favor to his subjects and protects them through the transformations of name and form. || 135 ||
In each respective state, that very [state] is the cause to be produced;
for that which is called the body of Brahmā, characterized by a predominance of *sattva*, is the form of Puruṣa. || 136 ||
In this period of Svāyambhuva Manu, that pervasive Lord was born as his portion;
he was first produced from the mind of Ākūti.
Then again, when the Svārociṣa interval had arrived, that very deity was born in Tuṣitā together with the Tuṣita gods as Ajita. || 138 ||
Furthermore, in the interval between the two Uttamas, he indeed became Ajita;
and in the Satya [Manvantara], he was Satya, together with the most excellent of the truthful gods. || 139 ||
And when the interval of Tāmasa had arrived once again, Hari himself indeed became Hari together with the monkeys in the womb of Hariṇī. || 140 ||
Furthermore, during the Cāriṣṇava interval, Hari was born again as Aṣa in Vikuṇṭhā together with the gods known as Ābhūtarajasas. 141.

When the Cākṣuṣa interval arrived, that god Vaikuṇṭha became Dharma Nārāyaṇa, together with the Sādhyas and the gods. But when the Vaivasvata interval arrived, he, Nārāyaṇa, [became] the Sādhyas. || 141 ||
From Kaśyapa and Mārīcā, Viṣṇu was indeed born of Aditi;
having conquered these worlds with three strides, Viṣṇu became Trivikrama.
That Lord bestowed [the sovereignty] upon Indra and the gods;
thus these seven forms of his have passed away through the seven past Manvantaras, by which the subjects were protected. || 143 ||
Since all this has been pervaded by him who was born here as Vāmana, he is therefore remembered as Viṣṇu, from the root *viś*, meaning "to enter. || 144 ||
Thus, the identity, the distinction, and the superiority of both Brahmā and the high-souled Vāmana have been proclaimed. || 145 ||

Those deities who are born here through a portion of the [great] deities are born equal to them in splendor, intelligence, sacred learning, and strength; indeed, they arise through the grace of those [deities]. || 146 ||
Whatever being is possessed of majesty, or endowed with beauty, or even with power, know that each of those has arisen from a portion of Viṣṇu’s splendor. || 147 ||
"He himself is born with a portion," so some men maintain; others, however, say that she is born from a mutual portion of him. || 148 ||
Arguing in this manner, they indeed speak by means of an illustration:
"Since there is no difference between the mind (manas) and the consciousness (cetas). || 149 ||
Therefore, because of that grace, they indeed become knowers of the field (kṣetrajña).
But the Lord, by the power of his sovereignty, becomes manifold while remaining one. || 149 ||
And because he, though being one, becomes manifold and then becomes one again, therefore from the differentiation of his radiant spirit (tejas), the various mental faculties (sumanasaḥ) are born.
In all the Manvantaras, the beings— both stationary and moving—
once produced at the beginning of creation, remain here by virtue of their merit;
yet, at the arrival of each Kalpa's end, Rudra withdraws all creatures.
The lords are born through their portions by means of their power of yoga-illusion, deluding [the world];
though they move about with sovereign power, they indeed delude those who lack such sovereignty. || 150 ||
Therefore, in their conduct, there is nothing that can be called either proper or improper.
Those who speak falsely about reality are miserable; those who speak of reality with impartiality are neutral. || 151 ||

The three Vedas are capable of restating what has already occurred for those who debate; yet he who does not accept them after examination, and accepts them through the opposite [lack of examination], [is at fault]. 152.
And because of having previously heard [false doctrines] with firm conviction, and because of worldly discourse, one does not find reality as it truly is due to these four causes. || 153 ||
Previously fixed upon another object, even though it has passed into another time, one does not perceive that other existing object due to aversion. || 153 ||
He who is the substance of the gods and he who is their quality;
he who is the performer of great deeds and he who is great by birth. (154)
Through these four reasons known from scripture, the one who is without perception (asaṃjñaka) understands those deities according to their specific divisions. || 156 ||
And they cite this here; and they cite these two verses here concerning the Lord of Yoga: [two verses concerning the Lord of Yoga]:
"The self's own reflections..."
And having attained the power of yoga, he may perform [these acts] for thousands of others, and he may act together with all of them. || 157 ||
Just as he attains all objects of sense while performing fierce austerities, so too may he withdraw them all again, just as the sun withdraws the hosts of luminous bodies. || 158 ||
## Section 2. Genealogy | Chapter 2. B. (Bd. II. 4.1–37; Vā.
67.1–47) Having heard these words of his, the ascetic sages of Naimiṣa questioned the most excellent one regarding the sequence of the narrative: || 1 ||
How were the gods born here during the seven Manvantaras?
They are headed by Indra and Viṣṇu, and they are the Ādityas of great splendor.
O Romaharṣaṇa, tell us all of this in detail! || 1 ||
Thus addressed by those exponents of the Veda, the disciplined charioteer, the best among speakers, replied as he had been questioned by the great seers: || 1 ||
Indeed, the Jaya deities were created from the mouth of Brahmā out of a desire for progeny;
they are all remembered here as having mantra-bodies throughout the various Manvantaras. || 1 ||
The New Moon sacrifice and the Full Moon sacrifice, the Bṛhat-sāman and the Rathantara-sāman, acquisition and successful acquisition, and intention—
these abide among those who have restrained themselves, having seen the fault in ritual actions.
But having seen that the fruit of actions is characterized by decay and excess, || 5 ||
Disgusted with rebirth, free from sloth, and devoid of the sense of "mine," they were detached, perceiving the faults [of worldly existence] and longing for non-birth. || 6 ||

Having abandoned wealth, dharma, and pleasure, they indeed remained steadfast, relying upon supreme knowledge; relying upon the knowledge of the Puruṣa, having condensed that [knowledge], they were well-established. Having withdrawn their radiance, they remained [there]. || 7 ||
But having understood their intention, Brahmā became enraged;
then his father, Brahmā, spoke to those dispirited gods: || 8 ||
"You have indeed been created by me here for the sake of progeny, and not otherwise;
'Procreate and perform sacrifices,' thus I spoke to you in the past. || 9 ||
For, disregarding my words, you have established yourselves in dispassion;
loathing your own birth, you did not welcome progeny.
And because you have laid down your actions out of a desire for immortality, you shall therefore undergo rebirth here only seven times. || 11 ||
Cursed by Brahmā, those gods indeed propitiated him:
"Forgive us, O Mahādeva, for that which was done out of ignorance, O All-pervading Lord! (12)
To them, who were bowing down with humility, Brahmā spoke again:
"In this world, who that has not been authorized by me deserves to exercise independence?"
Everything has been grasped by me; how could beings act according to their own will toward me, whether for good or for evil? (14)
Whatever exists in the world, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is pervaded by me, whose nature is intelligence; who in this world could deceive me? || 15 ||
Whatever the activities of living beings are, whatever they have contemplated, and whatever they have performed—all that is known to me. || 16 ||
By me has this entire world, both moving and stationary, been bound with the bond of hope; who here would venture to sever it? (17)
And since I have indeed manifested here for the sake of creation and not otherwise, who would be released from my will without undertaking actions here? (18)
Having thus addressed those gods who possess internalized consciousness,
he then looked at them again and spoke.
Prajāpati has declared that those deserving of punishment must certainly be punished. || 19 ||

Since you formerly made this renunciation with me in mind, let that effort which was made—though it has been fruitless and boundless—become fruitful and result in happiness; may you be born through a divine nature. || 20 ||
"O best of gods, your birth shall occur by your own will;
having attained perfection during the seven Manvantaras, you shall manifest yourselves. (21)
Likewise, among the gods of the Vaivasvata manvantara and those of the Svāyambhuva and others, Brahmā sang this ancient verse there: || 22 ||
The triple Veda is the source of all that consists of Brahman; it is the ancestral rite, austerity, sacrifice,
and the giving of gifts.
Having become these along with the eternal dusts,
the All-pervading Lord dwells in another exalted state. || 23 ||
Having thus stated the meaning of the verse,
he then spoke to the victorious gods:
"When the Vaivasvata interval has passed, you shall come here into my presence."
Then, when the Lord had vanished, the gods—free from fear from any quarter, endowed with powers such as atomization (aṇimā), and possessed of the strength of yoga—took refuge [in him]. || 26 ||
Then, cursed by him in his wrath,
they became the twelve unconquerable ones known as the Jayas.
Thus, they were made to resemble the Viśve-devas. || 27 ||
Then, when that Svāyambhuva creation had passed away, those very gods [arose]. || 28 ||
In Ajitā, the sons of Ruci were the twelve Ajitas. || 28 ||
Vidhi, the sages (munis), Kṣema, Nanda, and likewise Avyaya;
Prāṇa, Apāna, Sudhāman, Ṛtu, Śakti, Dhruva, and Sthiti. || 28 ||
Thus, all these twelve Ajitas are remembered as being of the mind;
and they were then considered to be partakers of the sacrifice along with the gods at the sacrificial rite. || 28 ||
Formerly in the Svāyambhuva interval, and again in the Svārociṣa interval, those gods known as the Prāṇas were called Tuṣitas; they were worthy of sacrifice. || 28 ||
Furthermore, those Tuṣita gods were born during the Svārociṣa interval;
they were reborn as the sons of Svārociṣa in the Tuṣita heaven. || 29 ||
The auspicious sons of Uttama Manu were born of Satyā;
therefore, the gods in that Auttama interval are known as the Satyas.
They became partakers of the sacrifice during the third Dvāpara interval;
however, when the Tāmasa interval arrived, those gods became Satyas once again.
Twelve sons indeed were born to Hariṇī from Tuṣita;
those gods, known as the Haris, then became partakers of the sacrificial offerings. || 31 ||
Then, when the Cāriṣṇava interval had arrived, those gods, the monkeys,
were born again as the Suras in Vikuṇṭhā from Cāriṣṇu.
Those gods known as the Vaikuṇṭhas existed during the interval of the fifth Manu;
thereafter, those very same Vaikuṇṭha gods attained [their status] during the Cākṣuṣa [Manvantara].

Twelve sons, devoid of righteousness, were born to Sādhyā. Then, when the Cākṣuṣa interval had come to an end and the creation of Vaivasvata Manu was about to begin once more, those very Sādhyas [reappeared]. || 34 ||
When the beginning of the first Tretā Yuga of the Vaivasvata Manvantara had arrived,
those twelve Ādityas, who were the gods of the preceding interval, were born again as portions of the Sādhyas through Aditi from Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci. || 35 ||
When these Sādhyas had arisen during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu, they were cursed by the Self-born (Brahmā) and were born as twelve immortals;
thus, through that curse, those very Jayas came into existence at that time.
The mortal who hears this account of the sevenfold origin shall always be victorious by the command of the gods;
and he who recites it with faith incurs no transgression. || 37 ||
Thus, these seven modes of conduct, characterized by the births of the gods, have been described by me to you today; what more do you wish to hear? || 38 ||
## Section 2. Genealogy | Chapter 2. C. (Bd. II. 5.1–106; Vā. 67.48–135.
The Sages said:
[Tell us] of the Daityas and Dānavas, and of the Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Of serpents, spirits, and piśācas; of beasts, birds, and plants. || 1 ||

because of that deed, he is remembered as Hiraṇyakaśipu. || 5 ||

In ancient times, there was a horse sacrifice of Kaśyapa at the holy Puṣkara,
graced by ṛṣis, deities, and gandharvas.
According to the most excellent rite, as prescribed for the commencement of the narrative and other formalities, five golden seats were indeed prepared in due order. || 8 ||

The golden seat that had been prepared there for the sake of the Hotṛ priest— || 10 ||

Diti, having entered into the state of wifehood, became pregnant; her fetus remained within her for ten thousand years.
Then that embryo, having emerged from the mother's womb, [saw] that golden seat which had been prepared for the sake of the Hotṛ priest. || 12 ||

The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu performed supreme austerity for a hundred thousand years, remaining without food with his head turned downwards. || 16 ||

Having completely conquered the gods through yoga, I have established myself as the sovereign of all deities;

The Dānavas, the Asuras, and the gods together with the Cāraṇas.

and may they be incapable of being slain, whether by wet or dry means.

Thus addressed, Brahmā then granted him the requested boon with a reservation:

O son of Diti, you have been chosen by him. || 19 ||
"Come now; the promise shall indeed be exactly so.
And having granted him his desire,"
Right there, he vanished.
"May the Dānavas, the Asuras, and the gods indeed become equal; for whatever great sovereignty belongs to Māruti,"
Let this boon be granted to me. || 18 ||
Thus addressed, Brahmā then granted him whatever he desired,
having bestowed upon him divine boons.
Right there, he vanished. || 19 ||
Then that Daitya also remained, having pervaded the entire world of moving and unmoving beings with his own majesty.
Possessing many forms, he is the conqueror of enemies. || 19 ||
He alone shines in the sky,
assuming the state of the moon and the sun;
he alone, having become the wind, and...
It blew constantly throughout the world. || 19 ||
He alone is the cowherd, the sheepherder, and the farmer;
he is the knower in all the worlds.
Likewise, one who explains the mantras; || 19 ||
He is the leader, the protector, the guardian, the initiated one, and the sacrificer;

Then they became drinkers of Soma. || 19 ||
Such is the power of this Daitya;
therefore, learn further!
Let everyone pay homage to him.

Long ago, O Daityas, this verse was sung here concerning Hiraṇyakaśipu:
"Whichever direction King Hiraṇyakaśipu looked toward," || 20 ||

And on the shore of the ocean, the omnipresent Lord performed intense austerities;

Enraged, he tore [them] with his claws; wet and dry claws are thus described.

## Section 2. Genealogy | Chapter 2 | D. (II. 6.1–39; Vā.
68.1–39) | Henceforth I shall proclaim the sons of Danu; listen!
There were great Asuras, famous in their lineage, who were the sons of Danu.
Led by Vipracitti, those hundred were fierce and possessed of great prowess. || 1 ||
They have all obtained boons and likewise performed intense austerities;
they are true to their word, valorous, cruel, and possessed of illusory powers.
The Dānavas were indeed possessed of great strength, yet they were non-sacrificers and hostile to the Brahmins.
Listen as I describe them all in order of their importance. (3)
Dvimūrdhan and Śambara, as well as Śaṅku, Nirāmaya, Śaṅkukarṇa, Vipāda, Gaveṣṭhīn, and Dundubhi. || 4 ||
Ayomukha, Maghavan, Kapila, Vāmana, as well as Mārīci, Akṣaka, Mahāmāya, Aśiras, and Bhṛśin. || 5 ||
Vikṣobha, Suketu, Ketuvīrya, Śatahrada, Indrajit, Viśvajit, as well as Bhadra and Devajit. || 6 ||
Ekacakra, the mighty-armed Tāraka of great strength, Vaiśvānara, Puloman, Prāpaṇa, and Mahāśiras; || 7 ||
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, Puruṇḍa, and the great asuras Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sūrya, Candramas, and Candratāpana. || 8 ||
Sūkṣma, Nicandra, Ūrṇanābha, Mahāgiri, Asiloman, Sukeśa, Śaṭha, Balaka, and Mada. (9)
Likewise, Gaganamūrdhā, Kumbhanābha, Mahodarāh, Pramadoha, Kupatha, and the powerful Hayagrīva; || 10 ||
Vaisṛpa, Savirūpākṣa, Supatha, Halāhala, Aja, Hiraṇmaya, Śatamāyu, and Śambara—these were the [daityas]. || 11 ||
Śarabha and Śalabha, as well as both Sūrya and Candramas—these two are remembered as the powerful ones among the Asuras and the Suras respectively. || 12 ||
Thus have the principal sons in the lineage of Danu been proclaimed;
their sons and grandsons are beyond counting and infinite. || 13 ||
Thus these are declared to be the Asuras, the Daityas, and likewise the Dānavas.
Svarbhānu is remembered as a Daitya, while Anubhānu was the son of Danu. || 14 ||
These, however, are the sons of Danu who are recorded as following his lineage:
Ekākṣa, Ṛṣabha, Ariṣṭa, Pralamba, and Naraka.
Indrabādhana, Keśin, Meru, Śambhu, Dhenuka, Gaveṣṭhin, Gavākṣa, and the powerful Tālaketu. || 16 ||
These are remembered as descendants of the sons of Danu who were invincible even to humans;
born from the union of Daityas and Dānavas, they possessed terrible prowess. || 17 ||
Now, these fourteen great asuras who were born from Siṃhikā as the sons of Vipracitti are known as the Saiṃhikeyas. || 18 ||
Śala and Śalabha, as well as Savyasācin; Ilvala and Namuci, as well as Vātāpi and Sitāṃsuka. || 19 ||
Harakalpa, Kālanābha, Bhauma, and Kanaka, as well as Rāhu—the eldest among them—were indeed the crushers of the sun and the moon. || 20 ||
Thus, these sons of Siṃhikā are difficult even for the gods to approach;
they are of a terrible lineage, cruel, and all of them are haters of Brahman.
Another ten thousand known as the Saimhikeya host were slain by the powerful Bhārgava, the son of Jamadagni. || 22 ||
Prabhā was the daughter of Svarbhānu, and Śacī was the daughter of Puloman; Upadānavī was the daughter of Jambha, and Śarmiṣṭhā was the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan. || 23 ||
Pulomā and Kālikā were both daughters of Vaiśvānara;
Nahuṣa was the son of Prabhā, and Jayanta was the son of Śacī. || 24 ||
Then Śarmiṣṭhā gave birth to Puru, and Upadānavī to Duṣyanta; these two, Pulomā and Kālikā, were indeed the daughters of Vaiśvānara. || 25 ||
Your two daughters, who have many offspring, were the wives of Mārīca; from them were born sixty thousand sons, the foremost among the Dānavas. || 26 ||
Likewise, there were fourteen others belonging to the inhabitants of Hiraṇyapura;
these Dānavas, the Paulomas and Kālakeyas, possessed exceedingly great strength. || 27 ||
Those who were invincible to the gods have been slain by Savyasācin. Six sons of great strength were born to Maya by Hemā: || 28 ||
Māyāvī and Dundubhi, Vṛṣa and likewise Mahiṣa, the Kālikās and the Ajakarṇas, and the maiden Mandodarī. || 29 ||
This creation of the Daityas and Dānavas has been proclaimed. Furthermore, the five sons of Anāyuṣā are remembered as being possessed of great strength: || 30 ||
Araru, Bala, Vṛtra, Vijvara, and likewise Vṛṣa;
and Araru’s son was the cruel great asura named Dhundhu. || 31 ||
At the word of Uttāṅka,
both the sons of Bala— possessing great heroism and incomparable splendor— were slain in the cave by Kuvalāśva.
Nikumbha and Cakravarman were that Karṇa in his previous birth;
and those two, Kālaka and Khara, were the two sons of Vijvara.
Furthermore, Vṛṣa had four sons who were performers of cruel deeds:
One who kills a Śrāddha, one who destroys a sacrifice, a killer of a Brāhmaṇa, and likewise a killer of an animal; || 34 ||
Indeed, O sons, you have been overtaken by a lack of life-force; learn also of Vṛtra!
The terrible breaths of Vṛtra were born as he fought with Indra. (35)
The Rākṣasas known by the name Bakas were possessed of great strength;
they are recorded as numbering one hundred thousand, and were followers of Mahendra. || 36 ||
All were knowers of Brahman, gentle, righteous, and subtle in form;
all those highly virtuous ones dwelt within the subjects. || 37 ||
This creation of the Daityas and Dānavas has been proclaimed.
Krodhā, moreover, gave birth to incomparable sons who were the best among singers. || 38 ||
Siddha, Pūrṇa, Bahvī, Vīryavān Pūrṇāṃśa,
and Brahmacārī are each ten times superior to the preceding one.
And Suparṇa is the seventh. || 39 ||
Viśvāvasu, Bhānu,
and Sucandra as the tenth—
these are the divine gandharvas.
These are proclaimed as belonging to Krodhā. || 40 ||
Flowing onward, she gave birth to sons who were indeed the best among singers at the sacrifice. || 38 ||
Satvanā, Sattvātmakeśa, Vīryavān Kalāpa,
Kṛtavīrya, and Brahmacārī.
And Supāṇḍu was the seventh. || 39 ||
Pana, Tarāṇya, and Sucandra as the tenth—
these are the Deva-gandharvas.
These are proclaimed as those who are to be known. || 40 ||
## Section 2. Genealogy | Chapter 2. E. (Bd. II. 7.443b–465a; Vā.
Surasā gave birth to one hundred serpents who bore heads [with multiple faces].
Takṣaka is the king of the sarpas, and Vāsuki is the king of the nāgas. || 1 ||
This group, characterized by an abundance of *tamas*, belongs to the lineage of Krodhavaśā;
they are the progeny of Pulaha—now learn of the offspring of Tāmrā! || 2 ||
Six daughters, moreover, were widely renowned as born of Tāmrā:
Śyenī, Bhāsī, Krauñcī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and likewise Śukī. (3)
And Aruṇa’s wife, the female vulture, gave birth to two heroic, mighty, and most excellent birds: Saṃpāti and Jaṭāyu.
The Vijayas were the sons of Sampāti; Sampāti begot a son named Prasaha from Dvīrāsyā, as well as one daughter. And the sons of Jaṭāyu were Kokagṛdhra and Aśvakarṇin.
The wives of Garuḍa were Bhāsī, Krauñcī, Śukī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Bhadrā; I shall now tell you of their offspring. || 6 ||
Śukī gave birth to six celebrated sons of Garuḍa.
Triśiras and Sumukha, Bala, Pṛṣṭha, and Mahābala; Sukha, Sunetra, Viśikha, Triśaṅkhanetra, and Sumukha.
Excellent form, excellent flavor, and strength. || 7 || Excellent form, excellent flavor, and strength. || 7 ||
The sons and grandsons of those high-souled Garuḍas were fourteen thousand in number— cruel devourers of serpents.
And I shall describe, in due order, those places which have been pervaded by the lineages of their descendants through the procreation of sons and grandsons. || 9 ||
The entire island of Śālmalidvīpa, the Devakūṭa mountain,
and Maṇimant, the lord of mountains with its thousand peaks.
Parṇamāla, Sukeśa, Śataśṛṅga, as well as Acala, Kauraja, Pañcaśikhara, and the Hemakūṭa mountain. || 11 ||
The mountain peaks were covered by those great-souled ones, who resembled Garuḍas, who were ablaze with the speed of fierce winds, and who possessed the hue of rubies. || 12 ||
The descendants of Bhāsī are known as the owls, crows, and cocks;
the peacocks, sparrows, pigeons, quails, and partridges. || 13 ||
The female curlew, the vādhriṇasa, the female hawk, the osprey, the crane, and the heron—these and other such carnivorous birds as well. || 14 ||
The passionate Dhṛtarāṣṭrī gave birth to swans,
ruddy geese, cakravāka birds, and all other water-dwelling twice-born birds.
He then produced these very ones, as well as an endless lineage of sons and grandsons.
These are declared to be the offspring of Garuḍa; now hear of the progeny of Irā! || 16 ||
Irā gave birth to three lotus-eyed daughters,
who were the mothers of forest trees, common trees, and creeping plants.
The creeper (latā), the non-creeper (alatā),
and the shrub (virudh)— these three were born from the Vanaspati.
Even from flowers, they bring forth fruit. || 18 ||
The fire-born woman gave birth to trees bearing flowers and fruits,
as well as shrubs, creepers, and climbing vines.
The species of grasses are the bark-fibers; and they are indeed classified as creepers, climbing plants,
and shrubs.
The creeper gave birth to forest trees that were flowerless and situated upon the sandy banks. || 18 ||
The creeper brought forth trees laden with flowers and fruits; then the climbing vine produced shrubs as well.
The species of grasses are the *tvaksāras*;
for they are the offspring of those creepers (*vīrudh*), and here the lineage comes to an end. || 19 ||
These descendants of Kaśyapa, both stationary and moving, have been explained;
their sons and grandsons by whom this world is perpetuated. || 20 ||

This single portion of a part of the creation has been recounted by me; this progeny of Mārīca has been described in brief. It is not possible to describe it in detail even in hundreds of years. || 21 ||
